14.0.0.en: 1- "The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God. They are corrupt, they have done abominable works, there is none that doeth good."

14.0.1.en: 1- Denying the existence of God is folly; because whoever denies God declares that his human nature is not immortal and will perish, so he lowers himself and makes himself like the animals.

14.0.2.en: And if God exists and he in his folly denies His existence, he exposes himself to punishment because of his corruption, so in both cases he is a fool.

14.0.3.en: 2- The fool denies God in his thought, and feels this in his heart, whether he declares it with his tongue or not; in both cases he is an atheist and a fool.

14.0.4.en: 3- The word "fool" in Hebrew is "nabal", or "withered", or "dry" like the leaves of autumn, meaning that he is worthless and his speech and life have no meaning; because he has lost God, the source of life.

14.0.5.en: 4- Denying God permits the fool to be immersed in corruption and evil and to keep away from goodness. And a person's immersion in evil makes him deny God, to justify and acquit himself so that his conscience does not prick him.

14.0.6.en: 5- The fool falls into weakness of mind and heart: the mind has not examined the Holy Scriptures and understood nature, so as to understand that God is behind it, and the heart has grown weak before the lusts of the world and become corrupt, that is, it has turned away from goodness and fallen into the abominations and filth of evil.

14.0.7.en: 6- The fool falls into many sins, the most important of which are:

14.0.8.en: a - He longs for God not to exist, so that he may continue in his evil; therefore he says "in his heart", that is, he flatters himself with the wish and longs for it.

14.0.9.en: b - When the fool denies the existence of God, he rushes into evil and corruption, without restraint.

14.0.10.en: c - If the fool denies the existence of God, he will therefore not ask for His help and will continue in his corruption and be unable to be rid of it.

14.0.11.en: d - The fool justifies his corruption and considers it among the natural characteristics of man, so as to be rid of the pricking of conscience.

14.0.12.en: e - If the fool sees the conduct of the righteous and his conscience begins to prick him, then he harms them; because in his view they are deviant, and in truth he is trying to do away with them, so that they do not rebuke his evil.

14.0.13.en: f - Whoever denies the existence of God will naturally not keep His commandments; so he does not do the good to which the commandments call, and because he does not believe in divine reward and punishment.

14.1.0.en: 2- "The Lord looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see if there were any that did understand, and seek God."

14.1.1.en: 1- Despite the spread of folly, David shows hope in God, who looks down from heaven, that is, watches the world; he expressed this in words that people understand, for God is the searcher of hearts and reins and does not need at any time to look down, because He always sees everything, but He gives us hope that God intervenes with perfect knowledge, and looks upon the folly spread in the world.

14.1.2.en: 2- God looked down from heaven, that is, from His loftiness and perfection; He is present everywhere, but heaven declares His loftiness, as we call Him in the Lord's Prayer, "Our Father which art in heaven."

14.1.3.en: 3- God seeks the person who knows Him with his mind, that is, who "understands", and longs for Him with his heart, so he seeks Him and searches for him, that is, "seeks", and so will find Him in the end. He looks with His divine eye upon His children who believe in Him and seek Him; they are not neglected in the midst of the many corrupt fools, and this shows God's care and concern for His children, even if their number is small.

14.1.4.en: 4- "God looks to see if there are any that understand" shows the fewness of those who believe in Him, since people are influenced by one another and walk in the way of corruption and the denial of God, and this of course grieves His heart.

14.2.0.en: 3- "They are all gone aside, they are all together become filthy: there is none that doeth good, no, not one."

14.2.1.en: 1- God saw that mankind in general had become corrupt and walked in evil and gone far from goodness, and there is not one of the atheists who does good.

14.2.2.en: 2- This does not mean that there is no person on earth who does not seek God, but it shows how widespread evil is.

14.2.3.en: 3- This verse shows that all mankind has fallen into evil, even the children of God, and needs the salvation which Christ offers in the fullness of time, whether these people are Jews or Gentiles, that is, believers in God or idol worshippers, as Paul the Apostle made clear in (Rom 3:10). That is, human nature has been corrupted by the Fall and needs the justification of Christ.

14.2.4.en: Remember the presence of God before you every morning, so that you may live in virtue and keep away from sin. And if you fall, hasten to repentance, for remembering God establishes His fear in your heart. Speak with Him in short prayers throughout the day, to remember His presence before you.

14.3.s.en: (2) The enmity of the wicked toward the righteous

14.3.0.en: 4- "Have all the workers of iniquity no knowledge? who eat up my people as they eat bread, and call not upon the Lord."

14.3.1.en: 1- David's question is not interrogative but denunciatory of the evil that the atheists do; indeed he rebukes them and threatens them with divine judgment upon them because of their evils in harming the righteous, and he answers them firmly in the next verse (v. 5).

14.3.2.en: 2- The wicked's denial of the existence of God makes them harm the righteous people of God, so they devour them and destroy them with all cruelty; because the wicked have denied God and His punishment.

14.3.3.en: 3- The wicked atheists go further in their cruelty, so they destroy the righteous in great numbers and with ease as though they were eating bread, and they feel no pricking in their consciences; because they have denied the existence of God and no longer call upon Him or pray to Him.

14.3.4.en: 4- It is understood from this verse that weak prayers make the heart hard and liable to harm others, and on the contrary whoever prays much, his conscience is refreshed, so it is tender and does not hurt the feelings of any person.

14.3.5.en: 5- Since the wicked do not call upon God they become proud and act on their own thoughts, which are evil, so they destroy everyone who does not please them, or seize his rights, because they have become without understanding or guidance from God.

14.3.6.en: 6- These wicked people who persist in their evil are like the false prophets, or the heretics, who lead the people of God astray, so they destroy it, and do not pray and call upon God so that He may guide them and turn them back from their error.

14.4.0.en: 5- "There were they in great fear: for God is in the generation of the righteous."

14.4.1.en: The wicked feared God, despite their persistence in evil, since their consciences have not died, that is, the voice of God is still in them and they try to silence it but cannot, and this frightens them. Why?

14.4.2.en: 1- Because He will take vengeance for all the evil they have done.

14.4.3.en: 2- They fear the loss of their position, their power and their possessions on earth.

14.4.4.en: 3- They feel the difficulty of repenting and being rid of their sins, in which they have lived a long time.

14.4.5.en: 4- They see God in the righteous and their sins are exposed, that is, the light of God in the righteous shows up their darkness, so they fear what they have done.

14.5.0.en: 6- "Ye have shamed the counsel of the poor, because the Lord is his refuge." (literally: you have contradicted the counsel of the poor, because the Lord is his refuge)

14.5.1.en: 1- So that the wicked atheists may continue in their evil they reject the opinion of the children of God, which declares the truth, in order to persist in their corruption.

14.5.2.en: 2- The poor man is the righteous man, who seems weak before the wicked, but is mighty and strong within; because God is his refuge.

14.5.3.en: 3- The poor man is also the humble man, that is, the poor in spirit, whom the proud try to dominate; because he is stronger than they, since God dwells in him, and so by his humility he rebukes them for their pride.

14.5.4.en: 4- This verse can apply to Christ, for He is the poor One who humbled Himself by His Incarnation and His Cross, and the priests, scribes and Pharisees contradicted His teachings; because they rebuke their evils.

14.5.5.en: Take refuge in God when afflictions come upon you, or when others trouble you, so that you may stand firm in your faith and God may support you, and so you are not shaken by evil, but remain in your prayers; so that you have compassion on the wicked and pray that they may repent.

14.6.0.en: 7- "Oh that the salvation of Israel were come out of Zion! when the Lord bringeth back the captivity of his people, Jacob shall rejoice, and Israel shall be glad."

14.6.1.en: 1- After David's review of the evil of the atheists he declares his longings for divine salvation by saying "Oh that", which comes from Zion, as God promised that from the seed of David the Savior would come.

14.6.2.en: 2- This verse is a prophecy about the return from captivity, which God accomplished in a miraculous manner at the beginning of the kingdom of Media and Persia at the hand of King Cyrus.

14.6.3.en: 3- The bringing back from captivity is not only from the Babylonian captivity but also from the captivity of sin, and this is accomplished through the salvation of Christ and the repentance of those who believe in Him and their return to Him.

14.6.4.en: 4- The salvation that comes out of Zion is not only through Christ the Redeemer on the Cross and His Resurrection, but also on the Day of Judgment, when Christ saves the righteous, His children, from the world and raises them to the Kingdom of Heaven.

14.6.5.en: 5- "Jacob shall rejoice, and Israel shall be glad": this is a symbol of the joy of Jacob, who has not yet met God and wrestled with Him but lives with Him, controlling his lusts and striving on his way, and of Israel, who wrestled with God and prevailed and whose name was changed to Israel, the joy of meeting God and fellowship with Him (Gen 32:22-32). That is, Jacob is a symbol of the ordinary believer and Israel a symbol of the saints who saw God clearly. And Jacob is also a symbol of the person who walks with God but is still in weakness and falls into various sins, while Israel is a symbol of the strong spiritual person who triumphs over sin, so the weak and the strong rejoice in God and both have a place in heaven, but each one in his own degree.

14.6.6.en: 6- The Jews believe that this verse is a prophecy about the Messiah the Savior and they are still awaiting Him until now; because they did not believe in the crucified Christ the Redeemer.

14.6.7.en: It is good that you ask for God's salvation from all your sins with faith and hope, whatever your falls, and thank God, who raises you up and forgives you and keeps you.

14.6.8.en: Dwelling with God. "Lord, who shall abide in thy tabernacle?"... (v. 1). Introduction:

14.6.9.en: 1- The writer of this psalm is David the prophet, as it is in its title.

14.6.11.en: a - When David celebrated the bringing back of the Ark to Jerusalem.

14.6.12.en: b - There is another opinion, which is that David wrote it when he was fleeing from the face of Absalom and Zadok the high priest came out to him, carrying the Ark, and he said to him, Take it back into Jerusalem, that it may keep the city, and if God wills for me to return to the kingdom, I will enjoy worshipping before Him; then he declared his longings for worship before the Ark during the period of his flight.

14.6.13.en: 3- This psalm was said at religious celebrations before the temple of God, so the visitor to the temple would say the first verse, which is a question about who deserves to dwell in the house of God, and the doorkeeper, that is, the guard, would answer him with the rest of the words of this psalm.

14.6.14.en: 4- If the previous psalm, that is, the fourteenth, speaks about the fool, this psalm tells us about the characteristics of the children of God, who deserve to enter and settle in His house.

14.6.15.en: 5- This psalm resembles the words of Isaiah the prophet in (Isa 33:15).

14.6.16.en: 6- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of Prime as number 14, because Psalms 9 and 10 are joined in the Septuagint translation from which the Agpeya was taken.

14.6.17.en: 7- David lists the characteristics of one who deserves to dwell in the house of the Lord, and these characteristics show the following:

14.6.18.en: a - Whoever worships God must have characteristics that confirm his purity and righteousness.

14.6.19.en: b - Some of these characteristics concern the feelings of the heart and some the tongue, and finally what concerns conduct.

14.6.20.en: c - David presents to us eleven characteristics of one who deserves to dwell in the house of God; six of them positive, mentioned in vv. 2 and 4, and five of them negative, mentioned in vv. 3 and 5.

15.0.0.en: 1- "Lord, who shall abide in thy tabernacle? who shall dwell in thy holy hill?"

15.0.1.en: 1- When David thought of those who enter and dwell in the house of the Lord, since inside it there were chambers in which the priests lived, in the days of Solomon, or tents in the days of David, he felt that God dwells and abides inside His house, and therefore the one who will dwell in the house of God must be distinguished by purity, and he wrote its manifestations in the following verses.

15.0.2.en: 2- When we feel God's dwelling in the Church of the New Testament inside His house we are filled with awe, and we even feel that no one can enter the Church except through the blood of Christ the Redeemer, that is, no one deserves to receive the Holy Sacraments unless he is a believer in Christ the Redeemer and has received His grace in the sacrament of Baptism. David speaks of all these matters in the spirit of prophecy in this psalm, looking to Christ, in whom the divine promises are fulfilled. For this reason, when the time for Communion of the Holy Mysteries draws near, the priest cries out in the Liturgy, declaring the awe and greatness of drawing near to God and receiving His Body and Blood, and says, "The Holies for the holy."

15.0.3.en: 3- If the heavens are not clean before God and He charges His angels with folly, who can dwell in His house? This is what David felt, so he presented the utmost he could of the characteristics of the righteous man here on earth, and in this he prepares himself to enter the divine presence in heaven.

15.0.4.en: 4- When David said "who shall abide in thy tabernacle" he meant a temporary stay; because the word "abide" in the Hebrew original means staying in a tent, that is, a temporary stay. But his saying "dwell" in the same verse means settling; because the word "dwell" in the Hebrew original is a verb meaning to settle. In this we understand that David is not repeating himself in this verse, but means that whoever stays in a tent beside the tabernacle of meeting, and then wishes to settle in the heavenly dwelling of God, must enjoy the following conditions. David does not mean only dwelling in the house of the Lord on earth, but also in heaven.

15.0.5.en: 5- Staying in a tent is during war, and therefore the words of the psalm mean that during our life on earth in the tent of this body we shall meet wars from Satan, but after this life we shall be transferred to the heavenly dwelling, in which we settle and the wars of the demons cease.

15.0.6.en: 6- David says "thy holy hill" because the mountain is a symbol of the summit of elevation above earthly things; whoever wants to settle in the house of God must rise above earthly things to receive heavenly things. And whoever has experienced staying with God in His house enjoys fellowship with Him, and so rises gradually up the mountain, and the summit of this mountain means the summit of the relationship with God, that is, dwelling with Him in heaven.

15.0.7.en: 7- Descending is also a symbol of God's condescension in dwelling by His Holy Spirit in the dwelling of our body, so that He may raise us up and we may settle with Him in the heavenly dwelling.

15.0.8.en: 8- If David wrote this psalm in celebration of the transfer of the Ark, perhaps he felt the greatness of God and the awe of drawing near to Him, as he was affected by the death of Uzzah, who touched the Ark (2 Sam 6:7).

15.1.0.en: 2- "He that walketh uprightly, and worketh righteousness, and speaketh the truth in his heart." (literally: he who walks in perfection, and works the truth, and speaks the truth in his heart)

15.1.1.en: This verse includes three positive characteristics, which are:

15.1.2.en: 1- He who walks in perfection, and this includes the following:

15.1.3.en: a - The first characteristic is a positive one and is also a practical conduct, and it means walking in all righteousness and not walking in one virtue.

15.1.4.en: b - And walking in perfection means the absence of blemish, as in the Septuagint translation (the Agpeya), and it means the absence of visible blemishes that cause others to stumble.

15.1.5.en: c - And the word "without blemish" in the Septuagint translation, in its Hebrew origin, was used in describing the lambs without blemish that were slain in the house of the Lord, and these lambs are a symbol of Christ the Lamb without blemish, and the meaning of this is that this characteristic means perfection and walking without blemish, that is, being like Christ in His life on earth.

15.1.6.en: d - He says "he who walks", and this means a continuing state; he continues walking in perfection and has not yet arrived at perfection, so he is careful to keep away from visible sins, and if he falls into them he repents quickly.

15.1.7.en: e - God is the Perfect One, so whoever walks in perfection is the one who lives in communion with God and strives toward Him every day.

15.1.8.en: 2- He who works the truth: this is the second characteristic, and by it is meant the following:

15.1.9.en: a - The truth is God, so he works by the commandments of God and all that pleases Him.

15.1.10.en: b - Truth also means justice, so he works with uprightness in all his dealings, favoring no one and wronging no one, imitating God.

15.1.11.en: c - He who works the truth, it is certain that he believes the truth within him and worships God faithfully, and this appears in his walking in the truth.

15.1.12.en: 3- He who speaks the truth in his heart: this is the third characteristic, and by it is meant the following:

15.1.13.en: a - That his heart is pure and he lives sincerely in the commandments of God and feels God within him.

15.1.14.en: b - He who lives with truth in his heart is pure and therefore deserves to see God (Mt 5), that is, to receive spiritual enlightenment, so God reveals Himself to him and gives him the enjoyment of fellowship with Him.

15.1.15.en: c - He who lives in his heart with truth, his speech is truthful, so his thought and feelings appear in his speech without hypocrisy, and then they appear finally in his deeds, that is, walking in perfection and truth.

15.1.16.en: And therefore he is not liable to fall into lying, as Gehazi fell when he lied to Elisha the prophet, because his heart was attached to the love of possessions, so he behaved badly by lying to Naaman the Syrian and took from him garments and silver, and then lied to Elisha (2 Kgs 5:25).

15.2.0.en: 3- "He that backbiteth not with his tongue, nor doeth evil to his neighbour, nor taketh up a reproach against his neighbour."

15.2.1.en: 1- This verse includes three negative characteristics of the righteous man who deserves to dwell in the house of the Lord.

15.2.2.en: 2- The fourth characteristic is "he does not backbite with his tongue", and this characteristic means the following:

15.2.3.en: a - He does not hunt for a fault in another and pass it on to others to set them against each other; he enjoys the love that covers others (1 Pet 4:8).

15.2.4.en: b - He does not slander a person with lies for the purpose of harming him, for this is a clear sin of lying, in addition to lack of love, as we mentioned.

15.2.5.en: c - A straightforward person who does not work with cunning in secret; he is bold and easy to deal with and therefore others love him.

15.2.6.en: 3- The fifth characteristic is "he does not do evil to his neighbour" and it includes the following:

15.2.7.en: a - His heart is full of love and all his dealings are good with his companions and those around him.

15.2.8.en: b - An unselfish person; just as he does not accept evil for himself he cannot do evil to others.

15.2.9.en: c - A faithful person who cannot betray his friend and do evil to him.

15.2.10.en: 4- The sixth characteristic is "he does not take up a reproach against his neighbour" and this characteristic means the following:

15.2.11.en: a - A loving and gentle person who does not accept hearing others reproached before him, that is, he refuses condemnation in all its forms against every person; because the neighbour, as Christ interpreted in the parable of the good Samaritan, is every person (Lk 10:29-37).

15.2.12.en: b - He does not reproach anyone else, that is, he does not judge others.

15.2.13.en: c - His heart is forgiving; if he hears a condemnation or reproach of another he ignores it and rejects it and prays for all, to keep the purity of his heart and his love for those around him.

15.3.0.en: 4- "In whose eyes a vile person is contemned; but he honoureth them that fear the Lord. He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not."

15.3.1.en: 1- This verse includes three positive characteristics by which the one who dwells in the house of the Lord is characterized.

15.3.2.en: 2- The seventh characteristic is "in whose eyes a vile person is contemned" and its meaning is the following:

15.3.3.en: a - He hates vice, that is, sin, and not the vile person, or the sinner, however enticing the sin.

15.3.4.en: b - The eyes of this righteous man are lifted toward heaven, so all the lusts of the world are despised and contemned before him.

15.3.5.en: c - He is not influenced by the position or authority of sinners and does not follow after them, but rejects their evils.

15.3.6.en: 3- The eighth characteristic is "he honoureth them that fear the Lord" and what is meant by it is the following:

15.3.7.en: a - He cares for the saints and the virtuous, to learn their virtues, and glorifies them and honors them.

15.3.8.en: b - He encourages the godly who fear the Lord, when they hold fast to virtue and endure the mockery of the wicked.

15.3.9.en: c - He fears God, so he loves those who fear Him and clings to them and becomes a disciple at their hands, as the saints did in both Testaments, such as Elisha's discipleship to Elijah, and Timothy's to Paul.

15.3.10.en: d - He loves God and sees Him in those who fear Him, even if they are despised by the wicked; he honors God when he honors those who fear Him.

15.3.11.en: 4- The ninth characteristic is "he that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not" and it means the following:

15.3.12.en: a - Swearing was permitted in the Old Testament, so whoever swears by something bears its consequence even if it brings harm upon him and does not go back on his word.

15.3.13.en: b - A truthful and faithful person in his speech, so others trust him and deal with him with reassurance.

15.3.14.en: c - He fears God, so he fulfills his oath, or his promise, whatever the sacrifice.

15.3.15.en: d - Not attached to material things, but the love of God and of others is better in his sight, whatever he spends or sacrifices.

15.4.0.en: 5- "He that putteth not out his money to usury, nor taketh reward against the innocent. He that doeth these things shall never be moved."

15.4.1.en: 1- This verse includes two negative characteristics, then a very comforting conclusion.

15.4.2.en: 2- The tenth characteristic is "he does not put out his silver to usury" and its meaning is the following:

15.4.3.en: a - He does not give a monetary loan of silver, or gold, or any possessions to a poor man and expect profits; he has compassion on the needy and helps them, or at least lends to them without benefiting from them.

15.4.4.en: b - Giving silver, or money, for the purpose of profit to banks, or companies so that they may trade with it, and they gain a part and give another part, is not wrong.

15.4.5.en: c - Silver is a symbol of the word of God, and this means that whoever puts out his silver to usury, that is, trades in the word of God, like one who preaches to receive honor and glorification from others, this is very wrong and cannot be done by the righteous who dwell in the house of the Lord.

15.4.6.en: d - Not attached to the love of money, but uses money to meet his expenses and the needs of those around him.

15.4.7.en: 3- The eleventh and last characteristic is "he does not take a bribe against the innocent" and it includes these meanings.

15.4.8.en: a - A just person who does not pervert justice because of a bribe (Ex 23:8).

15.4.9.en: b - A person who loves righteousness and encourages it, so he cannot harm the righteous, whatever the temptations of the bribe.

15.4.10.en: c - Not attached to the love of money, but loves the truth with all his heart.

15.4.11.en: 4- He concludes the psalm with this comforting statement, which is "he that doeth these things shall never be moved" and it means the following:

15.4.12.en: a - Whoever is distinguished by these characteristics enjoys inner peace and lives in reassurance.

15.4.13.en: b - This peace helps him to grow in his relationship with God and in spiritual joy, so he is rooted and established in God.

15.4.14.en: c - He is not moved, or troubled, since the wars of Satan become weak before him, that is, the devil does not prevail against him.

15.4.15.en: d - He enjoys this stability not only in this life but it extends to eternity in the Kingdom of Heaven.

15.4.16.en: Thus David concludes the psalm, that whoever enjoys these characteristics not only dwells in the house of the Lord, but goes beyond this with steadfastness for ever, that is, the enjoyment of God in this life, and then in heaven.

15.4.17.en: The way to the Kingdom is clear; if you love to be with God in eternity, then naturally you must enjoy fellowship with Him on earth, by keeping His commandments and keeping away from evil, so that you keep your inner peace all your days.

15.4.18.en: God is my portion. A golden psalm of David. "Preserve me, O God: for in thee do I put my trust"... (v. 1). Introduction:

15.4.19.en: 1- Its writer: David the prophet, and the New Testament also bore witness to this (Acts 2:25-31; 13:35).

15.4.21.en: When David was fleeing from the face of Saul, the spies of Saul told him the place of David and he hastened to him with a great army to seize him, and reached him. A mountain separated them, and David prayed, and there came to Saul one who told him of the Philistines' attack on the land, so he left David and went to fight the Philistines (1 Sam 23:19-29).

15.4.22.en: 3- We see in the title of this psalm "golden", and in the Septuagint translation "golden, on a pillar", and the meaning of this title is that the psalm was written in gold on a pillar, or a monument; for a monument is erected as an indication of victory.

15.4.23.en: 4- This psalm is considered among the Messianic psalms; if the second psalm, "Why do the nations rage", speaks of the eternity of Christ, then His birth in the fullness of time, and the eighth psalm, "O Lord our Lord"... speaks of the incarnate Christ, who glorifies man, then this psalm tells us how the risen Christ glorifies man.

15.4.24.en: 5- This psalm speaks of the Resurrection of Christ and therefore of the resurrection of man in Christ, to live with Him in the Kingdom while on earth until he reaches Him in heaven.

15.4.25.en: 6- This psalm is prayed in the prayer of Prime as number 15, and because it speaks of the Resurrection, it suits this hour, which symbolizes the Resurrection of Christ at dawn.
